title: Looking back: the hard century
hookLine: Banda, the forests, the ghallugharas, the misls

lines: THE CENTURY AFTER THE TENTH GURU.
cards: Cut limb from limb. Scalped. Broken on the wheel.
Sawn apart. Those words sit inside the Ardas, the prayer Sikhs say standing, in a long remembering of people who, it says, kept their faith and their hair to the last breath.

Every time the Ardas is said, in a home or a gurdwara, they are remembered again. Tradition ties those lines to martyrs of the century after the Tenth Guru. This year, slowly, this path told their stories.
Today, the hard century, seen whole.

teach.b: It starts with a servant. At Nanded, a Bairagi ascetic named Madho Das met Guru Gobind Singh and, tradition says, called himself the Guru's banda, his servant. The Guru sent him north with five arrows.
He took Sirhind, struck coins in the Gurus' names, and gave land to the farmers who worked it.
Then came the hunt: the hills, a starving siege in a mud fort, capture, the march to Delhi, and a death that tradition says he met without breaking.
Next, the forests. With rulers hunting them, Sikhs took to the jungles and the hills, on horseback, and tradition says they slipped out to visit the Harmandir at night when they could.
Bhai Mani Singh, Bhai Taru Singh, and others whose deaths stand behind those Ardas lines belong to this time. Then the ghallugharas, the name Sikhs give to the great killings.
At Kup Rahira, Sikhs remember how the Khalsa fought while keeping the women, children and elders in the middle, shielding the families as they moved. And through it all, the misls.
Even before the worst of the killings, the Sikhs had organized into bands of equals, each with its own chief, joined in the Dal Khalsa.
They met at Amritsar, and decisions taken there in the Guru's presence were called gurmata. By the end of the century, the hunted were holding the land.
A servant, the forests, the great killings, and bands of equals: the hard century.

how: The Ardas, said standing at the end of Sikh gatherings and prayers at home, includes a section remembering the martyrs and those who suffered for the faith; Sikhs also mark the ghallugharas and Banda Singh Bahadur's story on days in the calendar.

o: forgetting the past to make a fresh start
seeing the century Sikhs were hunted, yet held on
a wish to undo the battles of the past

games.q: the hard century — tap the pairs.
p: where hunted Sikhs lived on horseback
a decision taken together at Amritsar
bands of equals, each with a chief

s: the misls were ruled by one king
a misl was a band of equals with its own chief, joined to the others in the Dal Khalsa.
the Ardas itself remembers the martyrs of this time
near its end it names those who kept their faith through torture, and it is said again every time.
Banda was born into a Sikh family
he was a Bairagi ascetic named Madho Das when he met Guru Gobind Singh at Nanded.

games.q: the Sikh bands have no king, and a hard choice must be made for all of them. how is it decided?
o: they gather at Amritsar and decide together in the Guru's presence.
each band goes its own way.
games.why: the misls met at Amritsar, and decisions taken there together, in the Guru's presence, were called gurmata.

practice: The practice is the part of the Ardas that remembers the martyrs.

If you pray and know those lines, say them quietly now, in Punjabi or in your own understanding of them; if you don't, hold the picture in silence: the people of that century, the families in the middle of the ring, the ones who kept going.
Let each breath out be a small bow to them.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. Today at the century after the Tenth Guru: Banda's rise and death, the years in the forests, the ghallugharas, and the misls. Today's word.

orig.note: ghallughara, a great destruction: the name Sikhs give to the great killings of that century.

carryVoice: Your line: the hard century. Its people are still remembered, every time the Ardas is said. See you tomorrow.
